Content: Excess intracellular iron is toxic to cells (iron-induced toxicity). Ferritin is an intracellular iron storage protein that binds excess iron. The presence of ferritin can protect cells from iron-induced toxicity.

In an experiment to investigate the effects of dietary iron intake on ferritin synthesis, rats were given food containing different amounts of iron. Subsequently, the levels of ferritin protein in the liver were measured. The results are shown in Figure `1`.
:ibox:Figure `1`. Effects of dietary iron on ferritin levels in rat liver

Based on these and other data, researchers have developed the following model demonstrating how ferritin synthesis is regulated by iron. When iron levels are low, a repressor of translation, iron response protein (`text(IRP)`), binds to an iron response element (`text(IRE)`), which is a stem-loop structure near the `5'` end of ferritin `text(mRNA)`. When iron levels are high, intracellular iron binds to the `text(IRP)`, and the `text(iron-IRP)` complex dissociates from the `text(IRE)`, permitting ribosomes to proceed with the translation of ferritin `text(mRNA)`. Figure `2` represents the model of the regulation of ferritin `text(mRNA)` translation by iron.
:ibox:Figure `2`. Model of regulation of ferritin synthesis by iron
